claim: Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata domestica) sing variable syllable sequences.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata domestica), which sing variable syllable sequences, can learn to rapidly modify the probability of specific sequences (e.g. 'ab-c' versus 'ab-d') in response to arbitrary visual cues.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of the species used in the study.

claim: Bengalese finches can learn to rapidly modify the probability of specific syllable sequences in response to arbitrary visual cues.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata domestica), which sing variable syllable sequences, can learn to rapidly modify the probability of specific sequences (e.g. 'ab-c' versus 'ab-d') in response to arbitrary visual cues.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Modulation of syllable sequencing in Bengalese finches occurs immediately following changes in contextual cues.
source: Moreover, once learned, this modulation of sequencing occurs immediately following changes in contextual cues and persists without external reinforcement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 showing immediate shifts at context switches.

claim: Learned contextual control over syllable sequencing in Bengalese finches persists without external reinforcement.
source: Moreover, once learned, this modulation of sequencing occurs immediately following changes in contextual cues and persists without external reinforcement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by probe block experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Songbirds have a capacity for learned contextual control over syllable sequencing that parallels human cognitive control over syllable sequencing in speech.
source: Our findings reveal a capacity in songbirds for learned contextual control over syllable sequencing that parallels human cognitive control over syllable sequencing in speech.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Humans have unparalleled control over their vocal output with capacity to reorder learned elements to produce endless combinations of vocal sequences.
source: Humans have unparalleled control over their vocal output, with a capacity to reorder a limited number of learned elements to produce an endless combination of vocal sequences that are appropriate for current contextual demands (Hauser et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: Cognitive control over vocal production in humans is thought to rely on direct innervation of brainstem and midbrain vocal networks by executive control structures in the frontal cortex.
source: This cognitive control over vocal production is thought to rely on the direct innervation of brainstem and midbrain vocal networks by executive control structures in the frontal cortex, which have become more elaborate over the course of primate evolution (Hage and Nieder, 2016; Simonyan and Horwitz, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as current scientific understanding with citations to support it.

claim: Nonhuman primates have comparatively limited flexibility of vocal production.
source: However, because of the comparatively limited flexibility of vocal production in nonhuman primates (Nieder and Mooney, 2020), the evolutionary and neural circuit mechanisms that have enabled the development of this flexibility remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Song learning in songbirds exhibits many parallels to human speech learning.
source: Song learning exhibits many parallels to human speech learning (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999); in particular, juveniles need to hear an adult tutor during a sensitive period, followed by a period of highly variable sensory-motor exploration and practice, during which auditory feedback is used to arrive at a precise imitation of the tutor song (Brainard and Doupe, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Juvenile songbirds need to hear an adult tutor during a sensitive period for song learning.
source: Song learning exhibits many parallels to human speech learning (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999); in particular, juveniles need to hear an adult tutor during a sensitive period, followed by a period of highly variable sensory-motor exploration and practice, during which auditory feedback is used to arrive at a precise imitation of the tutor song (Brainard and Doupe, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The songbird vocal control network includes strong projections directly from cortical (pallial) to brainstem vocal control centers.
source: Moreover, as in humans, this vocal control network includes strong projections directly from cortical (pallial) to brainstem vocal control centers (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Simonyan and Horwitz, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Songbirds can rapidly alter aspects of their song, including syllable sequencing and selection of song types, in natural settings such as territorial counter-singing or female-directed courtship song.
source: Contextual variation of song in natural settings, such as territorial counter-singing or female-directed courtship song, indicate that songbirds can rapidly alter aspects of their song, including syllable sequencing and selection of song types (Chen et al., 2016; Heinig et al., 2014; King and McGregor, 2016; Sakata et al., 2008; Searcy and Beecher, 2009; Trillo and Vehrencamp, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Modulation of song structure by social context is often described as affectively controlled.
source: However, such modulation of song structure is often described as affectively controlled (Berwick et al., 2011; Nieder and Mooney, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The presence of potential mates or rivals elicits a global and unlearned modulation of song intensity.
source: For example, the presence of potential mates or rivals elicits a global and unlearned modulation of song intensity (James et al., 2018) related to the singer's level of arousal or aggression (Alcami et al., 2021; Heinig et al., 2014; Jaffe and Brainard, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Each Bengalese finch song repertoire includes approximately 5-12 acoustically distinct syllables.
source: Each Bengalese finch song repertoire includes ~5–12 acoustically distinct elements ('syllables') that are strung together into sequences in variable but non-random order.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the species.

claim: The relative probabilities of specific transitions between syllables normally remain constant over time in Bengalese finches.
source: For a given bird, the relative probabilities of specific transitions between syllables normally remain constant over time (Okanoya, 2004; Warren et al., 2012), but previous work has shown that birds can gradually adjust the probabilities of alternative sequences in response to training that reinforces the production of some sequences over others.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Birds can gradually adjust the probabilities of alternative sequences in response to training that reinforces the production of some sequences over others.
source: For a given bird, the relative probabilities of specific transitions between syllables normally remain constant over time (Okanoya, 2004; Warren et al., 2012), but previous work has shown that birds can gradually adjust the probabilities of alternative sequences in response to training that reinforces the production of some sequences over others.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Changes to syllable sequencing in response to reinforcement training develop over a period of hours to days.
source: In this case, changes to syllable sequencing develop over a period of hours to days (Warren et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A bird exposed to aversive white noise feedback after a target sequence learned to gradually decrease the relative probability of that sequence over a period of days.
source: In response, the bird learned over a period of days to gradually decrease the relative probability of that sequence in favor of the alternative sequence 'ab-c' (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At baseline, switches between yellow and green contexts did not lead to significant changes in the relative proportion of target sequences.
source: At baseline, without WN, switches between yellow and green contexts (at random intervals of 0.5–1.5 hr) did not lead to significant changes in the relative proportion of the target sequences, indicating that there was no inherent influence of the light cues on sequence probabilities (Figure 1F, p(ab-d) in yellow vs. green context was 67 ± 1.6% vs. 64 ± 1.5%, p=0.17, rank-sum test, n = 53 context blocks from baseline period).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: After 2 weeks of context-specific training, significant sequencing differences developed between light contexts that were appropriate to reduce aversive feedback in each context.
source: After 2 weeks of such context-specific training, significant sequencing differences developed between light contexts that were appropriate to reduce aversive feedback in each context (Figure 1G, p(ab-d) in yellow vs. green context shifted to 36.5 ± 4.8% vs. 83.1 ± 3.5%, p<0.01, rank-sum test, n = 22 context blocks, block duration between 1 and 2.5 hr).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: For all eight birds trained on the context-dependent protocol, context-dependent sequencing differences developed in the appropriate direction over a period of weeks.
source: Likewise, for all birds trained on this protocol (n = 8), context-dependent sequencing differences developed in the appropriate direction over a period of weeks (27 ± 6% difference in probabilities between contexts after a mean of 33 days training, versus 1% ± 2% average difference in probabilities at baseline; p<0.01, n = 8, signed rank test, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Across all birds, switches to the yellow context were accompanied by an immediate decrease in the probability of the yellow target sequence.
source: This 'switch-triggered average' revealed that across all birds, switches to the yellow context were accompanied by an immediate decrease in the probability of the yellow target sequence, whereas switches out of the yellow context (and into the green context) led to an immediate increase in the yellow target sequence (Figure 2C,D, p<0.05, signed rank test comparing first and last song, n = 8).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Switches out of the yellow context led to an immediate increase in the yellow target sequence.
source: This 'switch-triggered average' revealed that across all birds, switches to the yellow context were accompanied by an immediate decrease in the probability of the yellow target sequence, whereas switches out of the yellow context (and into the green context) led to an immediate increase in the yellow target sequence (Figure 2C,D, p<0.05, signed rank test comparing first and last song, n = 8).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The immediate shift in sequence probability averaged 0.24 ± 0.06 for switches to green light and −0.22 ± 0.06 for switches to yellow light.
source: To quantify the size of these immediate shifts, we calculated the difference in sequence probability from the last five songs in the previous context to the first five songs in the current context; this difference averaged 0.24 ± 0.06 for switches to green light and −0.22 ± 0.06 for switches to yellow light (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is stated with quantitative measurements and shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Birds can learn to immediately recall an acquired memory of context-appropriate sequencing upon entry into each context, even before having the chance to learn from reinforcing feedback within that context.
source: These results indicate that birds could learn to immediately recall an acquired memory of context-appropriate sequencing upon entry into each context, even before having the chance to learn from reinforcing feedback within that context.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immediate shift data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The magnitude of the immediate shift at the onset of blocks increased over the course of training.
source: Over the course of training, the immediate shift at the onset of each block got larger, while the gradual change within blocks stayed approximately the same (learning trajectories remained parallel over training, Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The rate of change in sequence probability within blocks stayed constant over the course of training.
source: Over the course of training, the immediate shift at the onset of each block got larger, while the gradual change within blocks stayed approximately the same (learning trajectories remained parallel over training, Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The rate of learning within each block stayed constant over time for all five birds analyzed.
source: As for the example bird, we found that the rate of learning within each block stayed constant over time for all five birds (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The magnitude of immediate shifts increased over time for all birds.
source: In contrast, the magnitude of immediate shifts increased over time for all birds (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Adjustments to sequence probability reflect two dissociable processes: an immediate cue-dependent shift in sequence probability at the beginning of blocks that increases with contextual training, and a gradual adaptation of sequence probability within blocks that does not increase with contextual training.
source: These analyses indicate that adjustments to sequence probability reflect two dissociable processes, an immediate cue-dependent shift in sequence probability at the beginning of blocks, that increases with contextual training, and a gradual adaptation of sequence probability within blocks, that does not increase with contextual training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Light switches into probe blocks were associated with similar magnitude shifts in sequence probability as switches into white noise blocks of the corresponding color.
source: Light switches into probe blocks were associated with similar magnitude shifts in sequence probability as switches into WN blocks of the corresponding color (−0.22 ± 0.06 to both yellow WN and yellow probe blocks from green WN blocks, p=0.94, signed rank test; 0.24 ± 0.06 to green WN and 0.23 ± 0.07 to green probe blocks from yellow WN blocks, p=0.64, signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis.

claim: All eight birds showed immediate and appropriately directed shifts in sequencing at switches between probe blocks.
source: Similar immediate and appropriately directed shifts in sequencing at switches between probe blocks were observed for all eight birds (Figure 3E,F, p<0.05 signed rank test, n = 8), with average shifts in sequence probabilities of −0.21 ± 0.09 and 0.17 ± 0.08 (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3E,F,G,H.

claim: Visual cues alone are sufficient to cause anticipatory, learned shifts between syllable sequences.
source: The presence of such changes in the first songs sung after probe–probe switches indicates that visual cues alone are sufficient to cause anticipatory, learned shifts between syllable sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the probe-probe switch data.

claim: Contextual changes in transition probabilities were highly specific to the branch point immediately preceding the target sequences.
source: This difference matrix indicates that changes to transition probabilities were highly specific to the branch point immediately preceding the target sequences (specificity was defined as the proportion of total changes which could be attributed to the branch points immediately preceding target sequences; specificity for branch point 'aab' was 83.2%).
evidence: This is stated with quantitative analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Across all eight experiments, the median specificity of changes to the most proximal branch points was 84.95%.
source: Across all eight experiments, the median specificity of changes to the most proximal branch points was 84.95%, and only one bird, which was also the worst learner in the contextual training paradigm, had a specificity of less than 50% (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated with quantitative analysis and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Contextual changes were specific to target sequences and did not reflect global sequencing changes that characterize innate social modulation of song structure.
source: Hence, contextual changes were specific to target sequences and did not reflect the kind of global sequencing changes that characterize innate social modulation of song structure (Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the specificity analysis with citations.

claim: All three birds trained with three different color-cued contexts showed adaptive sequencing changes for the first song bout in probe blocks.
source: All birds (n = 3) showed adaptive sequencing changes for the first song bout in probe blocks (Figure 5B,C) as well as immediate shifts in the adaptive directions for all color contexts (Figure 5D, 0.11 ± 0.04 and 0.19 ± 0.05 for switches to green WN and green probe blocks, respectively; −0.15 ± 0.06 and −0.09 ± 0.02 for switches to yellow WN and yellow probe blocks, respectively).
evidence: This is stated with quantitative data and shown in Figure 5B,C,D.

claim: Birds can maintain at least two distinct sequencing states separate from a 'neutral' state and use specific associations between cue colors and sequencing states to rapidly shift sequencing in distinct directions for each context.
source: While additional data would be required to establish the number of distinct associations between contexts and sequencing states that can be learned, these findings suggest that birds can maintain at least two distinct sequencing states separate from a 'neutral' state and use specific associations between cue colors and sequencing states to rapidly shift sequencing in distinct directions for each context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the three-context experiment data.

claim: The ability to contextually control the ordering of learned vocal elements in songbirds parallels the human capacity to differentially sequence a fixed set of syllables in speech.
source: This ability to contextually control the ordering, or syntax, of specifically targeted syllable transitions within the overall structure of learned song parallels the human capacity to differentially sequence a fixed set of syllables in speech.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Animals including birds can be trained to control their vocalizations in an experimental setting by reinforcing the production of innate vocalizations in response to arbitrary cues to obtain food or water rewards.
source: Similarly, animals, including birds, can be trained to control their vocalizations in an experimental setting, by reinforcing the production of innate vocalizations in response to arbitrary cues to obtain food or water rewards (Brecht et al., 2019; Hage and Nieder, 2013; Nieder and Mooney, 2020; Reichmuth and Casey, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Songs produced in the context of courtship and territorial or aggressive encounters differ in acoustic structure from songs produced in isolation.
source: For example, songs produced in the context of courtship and territorial or aggressive encounters ('directed song') differ in acoustic structure from songs produced in isolation ('undirected song') (Sakata et al., 2008; Searcy and Beecher, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Directed songs exhibit faster tempo and greater stereotypy of both syllable structure and syllable sequencing than undirected songs.
source: This modulation of song structure by social context is characterized by global changes to the intensity of song production, with directed songs exhibiting faster tempo, and greater stereotypy of both syllable structure and syllable sequencing, than undirected songs (Sakata et al., 2008; Searcy and Beecher, 2009; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ethologically relevant modulation of song intensity may serve to communicate the singer's affective state, such as level of arousal or aggression.
source: This and other ethologically relevant modulation of song intensity may serve to communicate the singer's affective state, such as level of arousal or aggression (Alcami et al., 2021; Hedley et al., 2017; Heinig et al., 2014), and may largely reflect innate mechanisms (James et al., 2018; Kojima and Doupe, 2011) mediated by hypothalamic and neuromodulatory inputs to premotor regions (Berwick et al., 2011; Gadagkar et al., 2019; James et al., 2018; Nieder and Mooney, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some species of songbirds preferentially sing different song types depending on factors such as time of day, location of the singer, or the presence of an audience.
source: For example, some species of songbirds preferentially sing different song types depending on factors such as time of day, location of the singer, or the presence of an audience (Alcami et al., 2021; Hedley et al., 2017; King and McGregor, 2016; Searcy and Beecher, 2009; Trillo and Vehrencamp, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Birds with only a single song type, such as Bengalese finches, vary parameters of their song depending on social context, including the specific identity of the listener.
source: Even birds with only a single song type, such as Bengalese finches, vary parameters of their song depending on social context, including the specific identity of the listener (Chen et al., 2016; Heinig et al., 2014; Sakata et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The ability to contextually control vocalizations is relevant for the customization of vocal signatures for purposes of individual and group recognition.
source: The ability to contextually control vocalizations is also relevant for the customization of vocal signatures for purposes of individual and group recognition (Vignal et al., 2004) and to avoid overlap and enhance communication during vocal turn-taking and in response to environmental noises (Benichov and Vallentin, 2020; Brumm and Zollinger, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some of the contextual control observed in natural settings may rely on learned associations and other cognitive factors.
source: Our results indicate a latent capacity to integrate arbitrary sensory signals into the adaptive deployment of vocalizations in songbirds and suggest that some of the contextual control observed in natural settings may likewise rely on learned associations and other cognitive factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Evolutionary pressures to develop nuanced social communication may have led to the elaboration of cortical (pallial) control over brainstem vocal circuitry.
source: Perhaps evolutionary pressures to develop nuanced social communication led to the elaboration of cortical (pallial) control over brainstem vocal circuitry (Hage and Nieder, 2016), and thereby established a conduit that facilitated the integration of progressively more abstract cues and internal states in that control.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis with a citation.

claim: Human subjects can learn multiple 'states' of vocal motor adaptation and rapidly switch between them using contextual information.
source: For example, human subjects in both laboratory studies and natural settings can learn multiple 'states' of vocal motor adaptation and rapidly switch between them using contextual information (Houde and Jordan, 2002; Keough and Jones, 2011; Rochet-Capellan and Ostry, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Subjects can learn two separate states of motor adaptation for motor skills such as reaching and switch between them using cues or other cognitive strategies.
source: Similarly, subjects can learn two separate states of motor adaptation for other motor skills, such as reaching, and switch between them using cues or other cognitive strategies (Cunningham and Welch, 1994).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Models of context-dependent motor adaptation frequently assume at least two parallel processes, one that is more flexible and sensitive to contextual information, and a second that cannot readily be associated with contextual cues and is only gradually updated during motor adaptation.
source: Models of such context-dependent motor adaptation frequently assume at least two parallel processes (Abrahamse et al., 2013; Ashe et al., 2006; Green and Abutalebi, 2013; Hikosaka et al., 1999; Lee and Schweighofer, 2009; McDougle et al., 2016; Rochet-Capellan and Ostry, 2011; Wolpert et al., 2011), one that is more flexible, and sensitive to contextual information (McDougle et al., 2016), and a second that cannot readily be associated with contextual cues and is only gradually updated during motor adaptation (Howard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Contextual information can drive rapid shifts in adaptation at the beginning of new blocks, without affecting the rate of adaptation within blocks.
source: Specifically, in support of such a two-process model, Imamizu and Kawato, 2009 and Imamizu et al., 2007 found that contextual information can drive rapid shifts in adaptation at the beginning of new blocks, without affecting the rate of adaptation within blocks.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Contextual sequence learning in the Bengalese finch may be enabled by two distinct processes.
source: The similar separation in our study between rapid context-dependent shifts in sequence probability at the onset of blocks, and gradual adaptation within blocks that does not improve with training (Figure 2G–L), suggests that such contextual sequence learning in the Bengalese finch may also be enabled by two distinct processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2G-L.

claim: In humans, slow adaptation occurs primarily within primary motor structures, while fast context-dependent state switches engage more frontal areas involved in executive control.
source: Humans studies of two-process models suggest that slow adaptation occurs primarily within primary motor structures, while fast context-dependent state switches, including for cued switching between languages in bilinguals, engage more frontal areas involved in executive control (Bialystok, 2017; Blanco-Elorrieta and Pylkkänen, 2016; De Baene et al., 2015; Imamizu and Kawato, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The gradual adaptation of sequence probabilities within blocks in songbirds might be controlled by motor and premotor song control structures.
source: In songbirds, the gradual adaptation of sequence probabilities within blocks might likewise be controlled by motor and premotor song control structures, while visual contextual cues could be processed in avian structures analogous to mammalian prefrontal cortex, outside the song system.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Visual contextual cues could be processed in avian structures analogous to mammalian prefrontal cortex, outside the song system.
source: In songbirds, the gradual adaptation of sequence probabilities within blocks might likewise be controlled by motor and premotor song control structures, while visual contextual cues could be processed in avian structures analogous to mammalian prefrontal cortex, outside the song system.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: The association area nidopallium caudolaterale is activated by arbitrary visual cues that encode learned rules.
source: For example, the association area nidopallium caudolaterale (Güntürkün, 2005), is activated by arbitrary visual cues that encode learned rules (Veit and Nieder, 2013; Veit et al., 2015), and this or other avian association areas (Jarvis et al., 2013) may serve as an intermediate representation of the arbitrary contextual cues that can drive rapid learned shifts in syllable sequencing.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Current models of song production include networks of neurons in the vocal premotor nucleus HVC responsible for the temporal control of individual syllables, which are linked together by activity in a recurrent loop through brainstem vocal centers.
source: Current models of song production include networks of neurons in the vocal premotor nucleus HVC responsible for the temporal control of individual syllables, which are linked together by activity in a recurrent loop through brainstem vocal centers (Andalman et al., 2011; Ashmore et al., 2005; Cohen et al., 2020; Hamaguchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: One influential model posits that which syllable follows a branch point is determined by stochastic processes that depend on the strength of the connections between alternative syllable production networks, and thus dynamics local to HVC.
source: At branch points in songs with variable syllable sequencing, one influential model posits that which syllable follows a branch point is determined by stochastic processes that depend on the strength of the connections between alternative syllable production networks, and thus dynamics local to HVC (Jin, 2009; Jin and Kozhevnikov, 2011; Troyer et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The song system has the capacity to maintain distinct representations of transition probabilities and can immediately switch between those in response to visual cues.
source: However, our results demonstrate that there is not a single set of relatively fixed transition probabilities that undergo gradual adjustments, as could be captured in synaptic connectivity of branched syllable control networks. Rather, the song system has the capacity to maintain distinct representations of transition probabilities and can immediately switch between those in response to visual cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: HVC receives a variety of inputs that potentially could convey visual or cognitive influences on sequencing.
source: HVC receives a variety of inputs that potentially could convey such visual or cognitive influences on sequencing (Bischof and Engelage, 1985; Cynx, 1990; Seki et al., 2008; Ullrich et al., 2016; Wild, 1994), and one of these inputs, Nif, has previously been shown to be relevant for sequencing (Hosino and Okanoya, 2000; Vyssotski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Nif has previously been shown to be relevant for sequencing.
source: HVC receives a variety of inputs that potentially could convey such visual or cognitive influences on sequencing (Bischof and Engelage, 1985; Cynx, 1990; Seki et al., 2008; Ullrich et al., 2016; Wild, 1994), and one of these inputs, Nif, has previously been shown to be relevant for sequencing (Hosino and Okanoya, 2000; Vyssotski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The control of syllable sequence in Bengalese finches likely involves a mix of processes local to nuclei of the song motor pathway as well as inputs that convey a variety of sensory feedback and contextual information.
source: It therefore is likely that the control of syllable sequence in Bengalese finches involves a mix of processes local to nuclei of the song motor pathway (Basista et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017) as well as inputs that convey a variety of sensory feedback and contextual information.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citations.

claim: Eight adult male Bengalese finches were used in the experiments.
source: The experiments were carried out on eight adult male Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata) obtained from the lab's breeding colony (age range 128–320 days post-hatch, median 178 days, at start of experiment).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The age range of birds at the start of the experiment was 128-320 days post-hatch, with a median of 178 days.
source: The experiments were carried out on eight adult male Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata) obtained from the lab's breeding colony (age range 128–320 days post-hatch, median 178 days, at start of experiment).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The average template sensitivity across experiments was 91.3% (range 75.2-100%).
source: The average template sensitivity across experiments was 91.3% (range 75.2–100%).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The average template specificity was 96.7% (range 90.6-100%).
source: The average template specificity was 96.7% (range 90.6–100%).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The total duration of the experiment, consisting of baseline, training, and probe periods, was on average 52 days.
source: The total duration of the experiment, consisting of baseline, training, and probe periods, was on average 52 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Birds sang 226 (range 66-356) bouts per day during baseline days and 258 (range 171-368) bouts per day during the period of probe collection at the end of training.
source: During this period, birds sang 226 (range 66–356) bouts per day during baseline days and 258 (range 171–368) bouts per day during the period of probe collection at the end of training (14% increase).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Three birds were started on contextual training but never progressed to testing with probe blocks.
source: In addition to the eight birds that completed this training paradigm, three birds were started on contextual training but never progressed to testing with probe blocks, because they did not exhibit single-context learning (n = 1); because of technical issues with consistent targeting at branch points, (n = 1); or because they lost sequence variability during initial stages of training (n = 1); these birds are excluded from the results.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: None of the variables examined (bird's age, overall transition entropy of the song, transition entropy at the targeted branch points, distance between the WN target and the closest preceding branch point) were significantly correlated with the degree of contextual learning that birds expressed.
source: None of these variables were significantly correlated with the degree of contextual learning that birds expressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and consequently, all birds were treated as a single group in analysis and reporting of results.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
